title: Joseph's dream (Matthew 1:18–25)
hook: a quiet carpenter plans to leave quietly, then a dream tells him to stay

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Magnificat: Mary's song, where the mighty come down and the lowly are lifted.

A carpenter in a small town learns that the woman he's promised to is pregnant, and he knows the child isn't his. That's Joseph. After three days with Mary, all from Luke, Matthew's Gospel tells the same beginning from his side. In those days an engagement was almost a marriage: ending it took a divorce. Picture him that night. Everyone in a village that size will know soon. He could make it public, and let the whole village judge her. Matthew says Joseph is a just man, and he decides on something else. He'll end it quietly. No scene, no accusations. He has it all planned. Then he falls asleep.
screen: `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE STORY.` → `ENGAGED, AND SHE'S PREGNANT.` → `HE'LL LEAVE QUIETLY.`

segments.voice: Matthew says he was "minded to put her away privily." Privily means privately. It's already a kind act: he's protecting her even while he's hurt. But in the night, an angel comes to him in a dream: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The child's name will be Jesus, a name that means God saves. And Matthew adds an old line from the prophet Isaiah, about a child whose name is Emmanuel, "which being interpreted is, God with us." Matthew, like Luke, says Jesus had no human father, and he tells it through Joseph's dream. "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife." No argument. No speech. Joseph never says a single word in the Bible. He only listens and acts. He'll have more dreams in Matthew, and each time, he gets up and goes. He takes a child who isn't his by blood, names him, and raises him as his son, and that naming made Jesus a son of David's family line. Catholics call him the patron of the whole Church and keep his feast on March nineteenth. The Orthodox remember him as Joseph the Betrothed, soon after Christmas. Many Protestants hold him up as a picture of quiet, faithful fatherhood. A man who could have walked away, and nobody would have blamed him. He stayed.
screen: `HE PLANNED TO LEAVE PRIVILY.` · `FEAR NOT TO TAKE MARY.` · `JOSEPH NEVER SAYS A WORD.` · `HE NAMES THE CHILD.` · then, large: `THE QUIET ONES MATTER.`

segments.voice: Think of one kind thing you could skip today and nobody would blame you: the dishes someone else left, the text you could leave unanswered, the call to the relative who's hard work, the extra minute with someone who's lonely. Just picture yourself doing it quietly, without telling anyone. If you pray, you can ask for Joseph's kind of steadiness; if you don't, just let the picture settle.
Joseph's dream. A just man planning to leave quietly, told in the night: fear not. He woke up and stayed.
Your line: the quiet ones matter. Joseph's story has no lines, only choices. Forty days, done.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the Feast of Saint Joseph on March 19, and many honor him as patron of fathers, workers and the whole Church; the Orthodox remember him as Joseph the Betrothed in the days after Christmas.

original.note: Greek: a dream. Matthew says the angel came to Joseph kat' onar, in a dream.

trapdoor: what you thought: the quiet background character in the nativity scene.
what it means: a just man who planned to spare Mary, was told in a dream to stay, and did, without a word.
what a scholar hears: kat' onar, in a dream, appears in the New Testament only in Matthew: Joseph's dreams, the magi's, and Pilate's wife's. Joseph has four dreams, and obeys every one.

notes: Matthew's use of Isaiah 7:14 (Hebrew almah, Greek parthenos) is described, not discussed. A Keeper may want a note on the translation question in a later, deeper lesson.
'Joseph never says a word in the Bible': no speech of his is recorded in the Gospels; confirm.
Engagement-as-near-marriage requiring divorce is drawn from Matthew 1:19 itself ('put her away'); 'the law gives him ways to make it public' is general; confirm wording.
Pius IX named Joseph patron of the universal Church (1870); Orthodox commemoration on the Sunday after Nativity. Confirm.
Name Jesus (Yeshua) glossed as 'God saves'; Matthew 1:21 gives the reason 'he shall save his people from their sins'. Confirm the gloss.

Audit (10% sample): hook line 'the law gives him ways to make it public, to make sure the shame lands on her' cast the Torah as a shaming tool; replaced with 'He could make it public, and let the whole village judge her', which keeps the contrast with Joseph's choice without characterizing Jewish law.
